newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish troops in big push against Kurd rebels.
newsitem.headline: Turkish troops in big push against Kurd rebels.

text.p: Up to 20,000 troops backed by air power on Monday launched a huge drive against Kurdish rebels in the remote mountains of eastern Turkey, scene of a bitter 12-year-old conflict.
Military officials said about 250 Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels were cornered in a forest near the Ahvanos valley in the remote mountains of the Tunceli province.
Government troops killed six Kurdish fighters in the latest clashes and arrested one, villagers near the scene of the clashes said. There was no word on casualties among the security forces.

"Three Super Cobra helicopters and three warplanes bombed the area by noon, relying on information that the PKK was gearing up to ambush patrols in the area," a military official, who asked to remain anonymous, told Reuters.
Helicopters, including U.S.-made UH-1s, had been shuttling reinforcements into the rugged terrain since early on Monday.
"The bombardment is continuing. High numbers of PKK militants are cornered," the military official said.
More than 20,000 people have been killed since 1984 in the fighting, which has often spilled into northern Iraq.

Iraqi troops made their first incursion into northern Iraq in more than five years last month to intervene in the fighting between rival Kurdish factions. The move prompted U.S. missile strikes against Iraq and a large American military buildup in the Gulf.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller denied that Ankara would be ready to cancel a security zone it has declared in northern Iraq if Baghdad acted against PKK fighters based there.

"We are not ready to cancel the security zone because we fear the influx of refugees and the PKK has stationed themselves right next to our borders," she told reporters in New York before meeting U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.

The New York Times on Saturday quoted Ciller as saying in an interview that Turkey would be prepared to drop the security zone if Iraqi President Saddam Hussein was ready to "put an end to terrorist infiltration".

The anti-rebel fight costs Turkey around $8 million a year and blights its human rights record but successive governments have refused to negotiate the guerrillas' demands for Kurdish autonomy or independence.
The PKK has defied predictions by politicians and the military that it is close to defeat.
A cross-border drive into northern Iraq by 35,000 Turkish troops last year failed to budge the PKK from the region after six weeks of fighting.
Security officials said the latest push was also aimed at cutting off the rebels' food supplies ahead of the coming winter, when heavy snow often blankets the province.
Turkey regularly stations up to 40,000 troops in Tunceli, scene of a bitter Kurdish uprising in the 1930s and one the rebels' strongholds.

Security officials say they do not know if elusive rebel commander Semdin Sakik, also known as "Fingerless Zeki", is in Tunceli. Sakik has evaded numerous large-scale attempts to capture him in the province in the last two years.
